questions.question: Walter Sutton, a graduate student at Columbia University, watched the chromosomes of a large grasshopper under his microscope in 1902. Nearly all of them came in matched pairs, and as the grasshopper formed the cells that pass to its young, the two partners of each pair parted, one into each cell, just as Gregor Mendel's factors for a trait part. What did Sutton propose about the factors, later called genes?
questions.answer: Each chromosome carries many of them
choices: Each chromosome carries many of them
Each chromosome is just one of them
Every chromosome carries all of them
Only the chromosomes of sex cells carry them
questions.context: Sutton reasoned that an animal passes on far more traits than it has chromosomes, so one chromosome must carry many factors, and he set out the chromosome theory in 1903. Later work bore him out: each human chromosome carries hundreds to thousands of genes, each one a section of its long molecule of DNA, and Thomas Hunt Morgan's fruit flies showed from 1910 that genes really do ride on chromosomes.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (curriculum line G8.L2; NGSS LS3.A) teaches that genes are sections of DNA carried on the chromosomes, many genes to each chromosome, and the chromosome theory is the experiment-led story of how that was found.

questions.question: Joe Hin Tjio, working in Albert Levan's laboratory at Lund in Sweden, studied human cells grown in the laboratory late in 1955. He stopped them partway through dividing with a drug called colchicine, swelled them in a weak salt solution and squashed them flat, so that the chromosomes lay apart, clear enough to count. Textbooks had printed another number for some thirty years. How many did he count in each cell?
choices: 46, in 23 pairs
48, in 24 pairs
44, in 22 pairs
23, none of them paired
questions.context: Almost every whole cell Tjio examined held 46 chromosomes: 22 matched pairs and one pair of sex chromosomes. Theophilus Painter's count of 48 from the early 1920s had stood for about thirty years, though Painter's chromosomes had clumped and overlapped and he had wavered between 46 and 48 himself. The other great apes do have 48.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (curriculum line G8.L2) teaches that human body cells hold 23 pairs of chromosomes, 46 in all; Tjio and Levan's count is how that number was settled.

questions.question: A karyotype is a photograph of the chromosomes from a single cell, cut apart and lined up in matching pairs by size and shape. In a girl's karyotype, the two chromosomes of every pair match each other in length and in the pattern of bands across them. Where did the two chromosomes of a pair come from?
questions.answer: One from her mother and one from her father
choices: One from her mother and one from her father
Both from one parent, a different one for each pair
One from a parent and the other a copy of it
Each a blend of her mother's and her father's
questions.context: Every pair holds one chromosome from the mother and one from the father, so a person carries two copies of nearly every gene, one from each parent. The partners match because they carry the same genes in the same order, though the versions of a gene on the two can differ. Neither partner is a copy of the other, and neither is a blend of the two parents.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (curriculum line G8.L2; NGSS LS3.B) teaches that an offspring receives one set of chromosomes from each parent, so each pair has one from each.

questions.question: Two sisters, born two years apart, have the same mother and father. One has blue eyes and the other brown, and their faces are quite unlike. What explains the difference between them?
questions.answer: Each got a different half of each parent's genes
choices: Each got a different half of each parent's genes
Each got genes that changed as she grew up
Each got the same genes, but they showed differently
Each got more genes from the parent she looks like
questions.context: Each parent carries two copies of nearly every gene and passes one copy of each, chosen by chance, to each child, so each sister got her own half of her mother's genes and her own half of her father's. Full sisters share about half of their DNA on average; only identical twins share all of it. Each girl got 23 chromosomes from each parent, whichever one she looks like, and she keeps the genes she was born with: her eye colour comes from them.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (NGSS LS3.B) teaches that each parent contributes half of the genes, at random, which is why brothers and sisters differ; the mechanism (meiosis) waits for 9th grade.

questions.question: Nettie Stevens showed in 1905 that a mealworm's sex follows one pair of its chromosomes. Humans have such a pair too: one sex carries two X chromosomes, and the other carries one X and one Y. Whose chromosome decides whether a child is male or female?
questions.answer: The father's, for he carries an X and a Y
choices: The father's, for he carries an X and a Y
The mother's, for she carries an X and a Y
The mother's, for she carries two X chromosomes
The father's, for he carries two X chromosomes
questions.context: A mother carries two X chromosomes, so every child gets an X from her. A father carries an X and a Y and passes on one or the other: a child who gets his X is XX and female, and one who gets his Y is XY and male. Stevens had seen the same kind of pair in mealworms, 20 large chromosomes in a female's cells and 19 large and one small in a male's, when many biologists still thought an animal's surroundings settled its sex as it grew.
questions.grade_note: 8th-grade genetics (curriculum line G8.L2) teaches the sex chromosomes, XX in females and XY in males, as one of the 23 pairs; Stevens's mealworms are how they were found.

questions.question: Hermann Muller struck fruit flies with X-rays at the University of Texas in 1926, and he bred them beside flies that had no X-rays at all. Among the young of both, he searched for new inherited changes that had not been in their parents, such as white eyes or small wings. How did the young of the X-rayed flies compare with the others?
questions.answer: Far more of them showed new inherited changes
choices: Far more of them showed new inherited changes
About as many showed new inherited changes
Fewer showed them, since the X-rays killed the weakest
None showed them, since X-rays harm only the fly struck
questions.context: The X-rayed flies' young showed new inherited changes far more often than the untreated flies' young: about 150 times as many deadly mutations, and many of the visible ones were the same white eyes and small wings that turn up now and then on their own. The X-rays reached the cells that pass to the young, so the harm did not stay with the fly struck. Most of the changes Muller made harmed the flies, and he won the 1946 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for showing that radiation can change genes.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (curriculum line G8.L2; NGSS LS3.B) teaches that a mutation is a change in a gene and that genetic information can be altered by mutations; Muller's flies showed one cause.

questions.question: Ernest Irons, a young doctor in Chicago, looked at the blood of a dental student from Grenada and saw red blood cells bent into long, curved sickle shapes, and James Herrick reported the case in 1910. Such stiff cells jam in small blood vessels and cause bouts of severe pain. Doctors later found that sickle-cell disease is inherited. What causes it?
questions.answer: A change in a single gene
choices: A change in a single gene
Changes in many genes at once
An extra copy of one chromosome
A chromosome missing from each cell
questions.context: Sickle-cell disease comes from one small change in a single gene, a gene for haemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen in red blood cells; a person who inherits the changed gene from both parents has the disease. It is a plain case of a harmful mutation. An extra or a missing chromosome, by contrast, adds or takes away copies of hundreds of genes at once.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (curriculum line G8.L2; NGSS MS-LS3-1) teaches that a mutation can be harmful, and sickle-cell disease is the standard example of harm from a single changed gene.

questions.question: Sickle-cell disease strikes children who inherit the changed gene from both parents, and where there is little medical care, half or more of them die before the age of five. Yet when Anthony Allison tested nearly 5,000 people in East Africa in the early 1950s, more than a fifth of those on the coast, where malaria was common, carried the gene. Why had it stayed so common there?
questions.answer: Carriers of one copy survive malaria better
choices: Carriers of one copy survive malaria better
Malaria changes the gene in people's cells
Mosquitoes carry the gene from person to person
Every carrier passes it on to every child
questions.context: A child with one copy of the gene has the sickle-cell trait, usually with no illness, and is far better protected against deadly malaria; Allison found such children had fewer malaria parasites in their blood. Where malaria kills many children, more carriers survive to pass the gene on, so it stays common, though two copies cause the disease. Malaria does not make the gene and mosquitoes do not spread it: it passes only from parent to child, and each child of a carrier has an even chance of getting it from that parent.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (NGSS MS-LS3-1) teaches that a mutation can be harmful, helpful or neutral; the sickle-cell gene, harmful in two copies and protective against malaria in one, is the classic case.

questions.question: A nectarine is a fruit with smooth, shiny skin, much like a peach without its fuzz, and it grows on a tree much like a peach tree. Its smooth skin is an inherited trait, passed down from parent trees to the trees grown from their seeds. Where did the nectarine come from?
questions.answer: Peaches, through a change in one gene
choices: Peaches, through a change in one gene
Peaches, through a doubling of their chromosomes
Peaches, crossed long ago with plums
Peaches, crossed long ago with apricots
questions.context: Nectarines and peaches are one species, and the smooth skin comes from a change in one gene that the fuzz needs; a study of that gene points to a single mutation, long ago, as the start of every nectarine. Nectarines have been grown in China for over 2,000 years. The belief that a nectarine is a peach crossed with a plum is a myth, and a nectarine tree carries a peach's own eight pairs of chromosomes, not a doubled set.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (curriculum line G8.L2; NGSS LS3.B) teaches that mutations, changes in genes, are a source of new inherited variation.

questions.question: The genes that set a girl's eye colour do their work in her irises, the coloured rings of her eyes, where they control how much dark pigment, called melanin, is made. A few cells scraped from inside her cheek lie on a microscope slide. Do those cheek cells carry her eye-colour genes?
questions.answer: Yes, for each nucleus holds all of her genes
choices: Yes, for each nucleus holds all of her genes
No, for each cell holds only the genes it uses
No, for those genes are kept only in her eyes
Yes, for her blood carries them in from her eyes
questions.context: Virtually every cell in the body holds a complete copy of the person's DNA in its nucleus, so a cheek cell carries the eye-colour genes even though it never uses them, and a scrape of cheek cells serves for genetic tests. Mature red blood cells have no nucleus and carry no genes at all. Charles Darwin once proposed that particles from every part of the body gather to pass on its traits, but Francis Galton's blood transfusions between rabbits found no sign of them.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (curriculum line G8.L2; NGSS LS3.A) teaches that genes sit on the chromosomes in the nucleus of a body's cells, a full set in each.

9960e29f5d.why: Judge (medium, tell): 'No chromosome carries any of them' was dead once the stem showed the pairs parting just as Mendel's factors part. It is replaced by 'Only the chromosomes of sex cells carry them', the belief that genes sit only in the reproductive cells (M1), which the stem's sex-cell scene makes tempting. Fact-check (optional, taken): the male grasshopper also has one unpaired chromosome, so the stem now says 'Nearly all of them came in matched pairs' (F23). Key and context unchanged.

e9d2375855.why: Fact-check (error): Tjio did not grow the cells himself; the cultures came from Rune Grubb's laboratory at Lund (F22). The stem now uses the lead's wording, 'studied human cells grown in the laboratory'. The context's 'Every whole cell' is now 'Almost every whole cell', since the 1956 paper reports a few single cells deviating (fact-check note). Judge (low): the 92-in-46-pairs choice was not taken, as a cell stopped mid-division holds doubled chromosomes and a student could defend 92; choices unchanged.

5f2318eb1d.why: Judge (medium, tell): two wrong choices were dead to an 8th grader ('all of her genes from one of the parents' and 'took after the parent she spent more time with'), so the key stood out as the only one with genes from both parents. They are replaced by two misconceptions that keep both parents in play: full sisters share the same genes (F13), and a child gets more genes from the parent she looks like (F4, F12: 23 chromosomes from each). The stem drops 'and neither is a twin', which pointed at the same-genes choice. Fact-check (optional, taken): 'two copies of nearly every gene', since a father has one X.

dbdb780159.why: Judge (high, clarity): the choices split on 'same' against 'new kinds' of change while the stem itself said 'new inherited changes', so two answers were defensible, and the kinds of change are past 8th grade. The choices now ride one axis, how often, keyed on the one clear finding: far more of the X-rayed flies' young showed new inherited changes (F17, about 150 times the deadly mutations). Wrong choices: about as many, fewer because X-rays killed the weakest, and none because X-ray harm stays with the fly struck (germline changes are inherited, F16). The context keeps 'many of the visible ones the same' in the judge's hedged form. Stem unchanged.

d6b5c6e4e0.why: Judge (medium, tell): 'Peaches, rubbed smooth for many years' was silly and ruled out by the stem's 'inherited trait', leaving the key the odd one out beside two crosses. It is replaced by 'Peaches, through a doubling of their chromosomes', a real way new crop varieties arise but not the nectarine's (peaches and nectarines have eight pairs, F24), so the choices come in two pairs, two changes within the peach and two crosses. The judge's 'changes in many genes' was not used: it would have repeated the single-against-many split that f7f7c7f3ac keys. Stem unchanged.
